lessons.title: Lesson 18: Present Progressive ~고 있다; To be Getting ~아/어지다

grammar.explanation: Attach ~고 있다 to an action verb stem to say an action is in progress right now ("I am ___ing"). Conjugate 있다 for tense: ~고 있었다 means "was ___ing". For honored subjects, ~고 계시다 is used instead.

examples.en: The monkey is eating a banana.
I am reading a novel now.
My friend is cutting paper with scissors.
Last night I was doing homework.

grammar.point: 살고 있다 / 알고 있다 / 가지고 있다
grammar.explanation: A few verbs describe ongoing states rather than one-off actions, and Koreans often put them in the ~고 있다 form. 살고 있다 means "to be living (somewhere)", 알고 있다 means "to know (already)", and 가지고 있다 means "to have/possess". The plain forms 살다, 알다, 가지다 are also fine, but the ~고 있다 versions are very common.

Verbs for getting into a position (앉다, 서다, 눕다) describe the moment of changing position. To describe the resulting state of being seated, standing or lying, use ~아/어 있다 instead of ~고 있다. ~고 있다 on these verbs would mean you are in the middle of sitting down or standing up.

examples.en: The students are sitting on chairs.
The teacher is standing in front of the desk.
The child is lying on the bed.

grammar.explanation: Adjectives cannot take ~고 있다 by themselves. To express a change of state ("to get colder", "to become clean"), add ~아/어지다 to the adjective stem; the result behaves like a verb. It can then be used in any tense, and even combined with ~고 있다 to say something is gradually getting that way.

examples.en: The sky gets brighter at dawn.

lessons.title: Lesson 19: Korean Comparatives and Superlatives: 더, 보다, 가장/제일

grammar.explanation: 더 is an adverb meaning "more". Place it before an adjective or verb to say something has a quality to a greater degree or happens more. Even without an explicit comparison, the listener understands something is being compared.

examples.en: I want to eat more ramen.

grammar.explanation: Attach ~보다 to the noun being compared against to mean "than". It is usually paired with 더, although 더 can be dropped because ~보다 already shows the comparison. The ~보다 phrase can appear before or after the subject.

examples.en: My younger sibling is taller than me.
This chair is more comfortable than that chair.
I like Korean food more than Western food.

grammar.explanation: 덜 is the opposite of 더 and means "less". It goes in the same position before the adjective or verb and can also be combined with ~보다.

examples.en: Today is less cold than yesterday.
I am less lazy than my older brother.

grammar.explanation: To form a superlative, put 가장 or 제일 before the adjective or verb. Both mean "the most"; 제일 is a bit more conversational and 가장 a bit more formal or written. The group being compared within is often marked with ~에서 or ~중에서.

examples.ko: 우리 반에서 민수가 키가 가장 커요.
examples.en: Minsu is the tallest in our class.

lessons.title: Lesson 20: Well and Poorly: 잘 and 못

vocab.en: to gain, to improve, to increase
to escape, to come out of
to escape, to go out of
to be round, to be spherical

grammar.explanation: With a noun object, 잘하다 means "to be good at" and 못하다 means "to be bad at" something. The skill is marked with the object particle ~을/를. These are single words, so they are written without a space.
잘 is an adverb meaning "well". Put it directly before a verb to say the action is done well or properly.

Putting 못 before a verb means the subject cannot or could not do the action, usually because of circumstances rather than choice (unlike 안, which is a simple negation). With 하다 verbs, 못 goes between the noun and 하다, e.g. 수영 못 해요.

examples.en: I can't go to school today.
I couldn't do my homework yesterday.

grammar.explanation: Adding ~지 못하다 to a verb stem has the same meaning as putting 못 in front of the verb. It sounds a bit more formal and is common in writing, and it works smoothly with long verbs.

examples.en: I can't go to class today.

grammar.explanation: Written as one word, 잘못 is a noun meaning "mistake/fault", or an adverb meaning "wrongly/by mistake". Written with a space, 잘 못 means "cannot do (something) well". The spacing changes the meaning, so pay attention to it.

lessons.title: Lesson 21: Asking Questions in Korean: Why, When, Where, Who

vocab.en: to check out of a hospital
to not be enough, to be lacking

grammar.explanation: A yes/no question does not need any change in structure. Just say a normal sentence with rising intonation at the end and write a question mark. This works in every tense, and the subject "you" is usually left out.

examples.en: Are you going to school tomorrow?

grammar.explanation: The formal ~ㅂ/습니다 ending becomes ~ㅂ/습니까 in questions. Use ~ㅂ니까 after a vowel stem and ~습니까 after a consonant stem. It works with past and future forms too and is the most formal way to ask.

examples.en: Did you go to the wedding yesterday?

grammar.explanation: ~니 replaces the casual ending to make an informal question, often used by adults speaking to children or close friends. It attaches directly to the stem in any tense (했니, 하니, 할 거니). A stem ending in ㄹ drops the ㄹ before ~니 (살다 becomes 사니).

examples.en: Are you reading a comic book?

grammar.explanation: Attach ~ㄴ/은가(요) to an adjective stem or to 이다 to ask a softer, gentler question about a present situation. Use ~ㄴ가 after a vowel and ~은가 after a consonant, the same as describing a noun. Adding 요 makes it polite.
~나(요) softens a question in the same way as ~ㄴ/은가(요), but it is mainly used with verbs and with 있다/없다. It can follow the past tense (~았/었나요). A ㄹ-final stem drops the ㄹ (알다 becomes 아나요).

examples.en: Has your friend already left the hospital?

grammar.explanation: 왜 is an adverb, so you can turn a statement into a question just by inserting it, usually near the start of the sentence. On its own, 왜? is also how people answer when someone calls their name, like "what?" in English.

examples.en: Why does that person regret it?

grammar.explanation: 언제 asks when something happens and is placed where the time word would go. Particles like ~부터 and ~까지 can attach to it ("since when", "until when"), and it can come before 이다 to ask when something is.

examples.en: Until when are you in the hospital?

grammar.explanation: 어디 asks where. ~에 is often left off, and 어디에서 is commonly shortened to 어디서. Use 어디예요 to ask where a place is, but to ask where a person or object is, use 어디에 있어요.
누구 works like a noun, so it goes where the person would go in the sentence: subject, object, or before 이다. When it is the subject with ~가, it contracts to 누가. As an object, it can take ~를 (누구를).

lessons.title: Lesson 22: Asking Questions in Korean: How, What, Which, How Many

vocab.en: a seat, a place to put something
to collect, to come and pick up
to go and then come back
to be short, to be brief

grammar.explanation: 어떻게 is an adverb meaning "how" (in what way). It goes before the verb, in the position where an adverb describing the manner would be.

examples.en: How do you read this word?
How do you get to school?
How do you make this food?

grammar.explanation: 어때요 comes from 어떻다 and asks for someone's opinion or impression: "How is ___?" The past form 어땠어요 asks how something was.
뭐 and 무엇 are pronouns meaning "what" and go where the unknown noun would be. 뭐 is conversational and 무엇 is more formal or written. With particles, 뭐가 is used as a subject and 뭘 (뭐를) as an object.

examples.en: What did you eat for lunch?

grammar.explanation: 무슨 is placed directly before a noun to ask "what ___" or "what kind of ___". It cannot stand alone like 뭐 can.

examples.en: What day of the week is it today?

grammar.explanation: 어떤 goes before a noun and asks "which" or "what kind of", focusing on the characteristics of the thing. In a statement, 어떤 can also mean "a certain" or "some" person or thing.

examples.en: What kind of person do you like?

grammar.explanation: 어느 goes before a noun and asks "which one" when choosing among a known set of options, such as countries or particular items.

examples.en: Which seat do you want to sit in?

grammar.explanation: To ask "how many", put 몇 before a counter, the same way you would put a number there. It also appears in set questions like 몇 시 (what time) and 몇 살 (how old). 며칠 means "how many days" or "what date".

examples.en: How many apples did you buy?
For how many days did you travel?

grammar.explanation: 얼마나 is an adverb asking about amount or degree: how much, how long, or how (adjective). Place it before the verb or adjective you are asking about.

examples.en: How much did you study Korean?

grammar.explanation: A question word that is the subject takes ~이/가, never ~은/는, because it marks unknown, new information. The answer normally uses ~이/가 as well, since it supplies that new information.

examples.en: This kimchi is the most delicious.

lessons.title: Lesson 23: ㅎ Irregular: Korean Colors, 이렇다, 그렇다 and 저렇다

vocab.en: to be revealed, to be shown

grammar.explanation: Most adjectives whose stem ends in ㅎ (colors like 빨갛다, and 이렇다/그렇다/저렇다) are irregular. Before ~아/어, the ㅎ disappears and the vowel turns into ㅐ (하얗다 becomes 하얘요, 노랗다 becomes 노래요). Before endings starting with ㄴ, the ㅎ simply drops (빨간, 노란). 좋다 is an exception and stays regular.

Basic colors exist as ㅎ-irregular adjectives (빨갛다, 노랗다, 파랗다, 하얗다, 까맣다). Every color can also be a noun ending in 색 ("color"), such as 빨간색, 초록색, 보라색 or 회색. The noun form can be used with 이다 or placed directly before another noun.

grammar.point: 이렇다 / 그렇다 / 저렇다 (like this / like that)
grammar.explanation: These adjectives mean "to be like this", "to be like that (near you or already mentioned)" and "to be like that (over there)". Before a noun they become 이런, 그런, 저런 ("this kind of"). With ~게 they become the adverbs 이렇게, 그렇게, 저렇게 ("in this way").

examples.en: I want to buy a shirt like this.
I heard a rumor like that.
I want to live in a house like that.

grammar.explanation: At the end of a sentence these words describe a situation as being "like this/that". 그래요 is a very common reply meaning "that's right", and 그래요? means "really?". 이래요 and 저래요 describe something being this or that way.

examples.en: Is the weather always like this?
That person is always like that.

grammar.explanation: ~의 marks possession, but in speech it is often left out between two nouns when the relationship is obvious, such as 친구 집 (friend's house). 저의 and 나의 usually contract to 제 and 내. When 의 is used as a particle, it is usually pronounced like 에.

examples.en: I went to my friend's house.
The teacher's book is on the desk.

vocab.en: to put, to set, to place something
to be nice, to be kind

grammar.explanation: After an amount of time, 전 means "ago". Because it refers to a time, ~에 is usually attached: 삼 년 전에 ("three years ago").

examples.ko: 저는 삼 년 전에 한국에 왔어요.
examples.en: I came to Korea three years ago.
My friend called five minutes ago.
I went to the police station two days ago.

grammar.explanation: Add ~기 전에 to a verb stem to say "before (doing)". The ~기 전에 clause has no tense of its own; the tense comes from the main clause at the end. In two-clause sentences, ~은/는 goes on the subject of the main clause, and the subject inside the ~기 전에 clause normally takes ~이/가.

examples.en: I wash my hands before eating.
I read a book before going to sleep.

examples.ko: 엄마가 오기 전에 저는 방을 치웠어요.
examples.en: Before mom came, I cleaned my room.

grammar.explanation: After an amount of time, 후 means "later" or "from now". Like 전, it usually takes ~에.

examples.en: I go on a business trip in three days.

grammar.explanation: To say "after doing", add ~ㄴ/은 to the verb stem (not ~기) and then 후에: ~ㄴ after a vowel, ~은 after a consonant. 다음에 can replace 후에 with the same meaning.

examples.en: After taking a bath, I slept.
After class ended, I met a friend.
After eating, I had some snacks.

grammar.explanation: 이래로 can replace 후에 in the ~ㄴ/은 후에 pattern to mean "since (doing)". It can also follow a point in time. It sounds formal and is not common in speech, where Koreans tend to rephrase with ~ㄴ/은 후에 or 부터.

examples.ko: 대학교를 졸업한 이래로 이 회사에서 일하고 있어요.
examples.en: Since graduating from university, I have been working at this company.
Since I started exercising, my muscles have grown.
I have been living in Korea since last year.

grammar.explanation: After an amount of time, 안 or 이내 with ~에 means "within" that period. 안에 is the everyday choice, and 이내에 sounds more formal.

examples.ko: 한 시간 안에 숙제를 끝낼 거예요.
examples.en: I will finish my homework within an hour.
I will arrive within ten minutes.
I have to pay the bill within a week.

lessons.title: Lesson 25: Anybody, Everybody, Somebody, Nobody, etc.

vocab.en: to go out with, to date
to be severe, to be extreme

grammar.explanation: 모든 goes before a noun to mean "every/all" (모든 것 = everything). Adding ~나 to a question word makes an "every-" word: 어디나 (everywhere), 언제나 (always, every time) and 누구나 (everyone).

Adding ~ㄴ가 to a question word makes an indefinite "some-" word: 뭔가 (something), 어딘가 (somewhere), 언젠가 (someday) and 누군가 (someone). They are used where the specific thing, place, time or person is unknown or unimportant.

examples.en: I want to go to Korea someday.

grammar.explanation: 아무 combined with ~나 means "any" in a positive sense, like "it doesn't matter which". Examples are 아무나 (anyone), 아무 거나 (anything), 아무 데나 (anywhere) and 아무 때나 (anytime).
With ~도 and a negative verb, 아무 forms "no-" words: 아무도 (nobody), 아무 것도 (nothing) and 아무 데도 (nowhere). The verb must be negated with 안, 못 or 없다.

examples.en: I didn't go anywhere on the weekend.

grammar.explanation: Attach ~마다 to a noun, often a time word, to mean "each" or "every". It shows that something repeats or applies to every member of the group.

examples.en: I go for a walk every day.
I go to my hometown every weekend.
